title: Concerns and Issues in Human Development
summary: The girl child is discriminated against from before birth: sons and husbands are fed first and girls get left-overs of poor quality and quantity; girl infants are breast-fed for a shorter time; sick girls are not taken to doctors, so many do not see their first birthday; girls are taken out of school early to help at home. This is a vicious cycle: lack of nutrition, poor health, no schooling, early marriage and early pregnancy with its problems, and poor health of the newborn. Education creates awareness, gives financial independence and confidence, and educated mothers look after their children's studies, help them develop good habits and values and solve their problems; it makes a better daughter-in-law, wife and mother, and benefits society.

Juvenile delinquency is violation of law by young people (a boy below 16 and a girl below 18 years) who as a rule cannot be punished by the law: forgery, violence, stealing, lying, suicide, sex crimes, drug peddling. Causes: poverty (children steal for comforts; sometimes parents encourage it), bad company, violence in media (delinquents shown as strong characters), parents' quarrels (insecurity), lack of play facilities, overcrowded homes with no privacy and early exposure to sex, and disappointments. Remedial: children are sent to a remand home for vocational training and reform. Preventive: remove poverty (loans at low interest, vocational training through voluntary organisations), parents spend time with children and develop good habits and values, and provide recreational facilities.

A child labourer is a child below 14 years working to earn a living. Causes: poverty, illiteracy and ignorance of parents, orphaned, abandoned or rejected children, nimble fingers and keen eyesight needed in crafts such as carpet weaving, and demand for cheap, silent and uncomplaining labour. Consequences: long hours (12–16) in uncomfortable postures causing permanent disability, unhygienic conditions and infectious diseases, missing school and illiteracy. Remedies: non-formal education and release for school hours, educating parents, medical facilities and health camps, and clean, well-ventilated working rooms with fewer hours. Socio-economically disadvantaged children live in extreme poverty and lack facilities for development; help them with education (free books, uniforms, scholarships, mid-day meals), vocational training, teaching skills and hygiene, donating old toys and books, educational games, nutritious snacks, craft and moral stories.

Physical disabilities: orthopaedic (malformed bones, lack of calcium and vitamin D, accidents; the Jaipur foot helped dancer Sudha Chandran; spastic children have stiff muscles), blindness (only some are born blind; vitamin A deficiency and injuries are causes; Braille; use a stick, touch to learn shapes; Surdas) and deafness and dumbness (children born deaf cannot hear their own voice so find language hard; causes: loud noise, ear infections, pins in the ears; hearing aids, lip reading, sign language). Help: early medical examination, special schools, substitutes (braces, artificial limbs), mixing with normal children, use of remaining senses and hearing aids; they need support, not sympathy. Mental retardation is delay in mental development caused by brain tumours, pesticide poisoning, lack of oxygen, birth injuries or accidents; guidelines: never call them stupid, let them do things themselves, teach self-help skills, involve them in simple household tasks and enrol them in special schools with vocational training.

RTIs are infections of the reproductive tract; STDs (syphilis, gonorrhoea) spread by sexual contact. AIDS is Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus, a retrovirus) which destroys white blood cells and weakens the immune system. Symptoms in HIV infected people: persistent fatigue, weight loss of at least 10%, night sweats, fever for weeks and diarrhoea for over a month; an asymptomatic period may last ten years or more; antibodies appear in 2 weeks to 3 months (test after 3 months and again after 6). Transmission: infected blood and instruments (needles, blades, tattooing, ear piercing), mother to child (about 30%), and unprotected sex (the most common route, 80–90%). HIV does not spread by shaking hands, body contact, sharing utensils, working or playing together, kissing and hugging, sleeping in the same room, sharing toilets or swimming pools.

The safe motherhood initiative aims to reduce maternal mortality and morbidity. Women should avoid pregnancy before 18 years and after 35–37 years; plan the family with a gap of more than two years between pregnancies and two or three children, using contraception: natural (rhythm, coitus interruptus), mechanical (condom; diaphragm and IUD or Copper T), chemical (jelly or pills) and surgical (vasectomy, tubectomy); take care during pregnancy (qualified nurse or doctor, a skilled person at delivery who can refer to a hospital, a clean cut and tied umbilical cord, early breast-feeding for natural immunity). Not a precaution: testing the sex of the unborn child.

objective: As a community health worker, you advise a young couple about safe motherhood. Choose two recommendations and give a reason for each: (i) Avoid pregnancy before 18 years and after 35 years. (ii) Plan frequent pregnancies to have more children early. (iii) Keep a gap of more than two years between two pregnancies. (iv) Medical check-ups during pregnancy are not essential.
(i) Avoid pregnancy before 18 and after 35: it is unsafe for the mother's and the child's health. (iii) Keep a gap of more than two years: the mother's body recovers and the child gets care.

Identify the two correct steps to help a mentally retarded child. (i) Teach self-help skills (ii) Enrol them in a regular school (iii) Teach him braille and sign language (iv) Involve him in simple household tasks.
State whether True or False and justify. (a) Mentally retarded children should be involved in simple household tasks. (b) Body contact in crowded places may cause HIV transmission.
(a) True: it keeps them occupied and makes them independent. (b) False: HIV does not spread by casual contact.
Match Column A with Column B. A: (a) Blind child (b) Deaf child. B: (i) Sign language and lip reading (ii) Braille and a stick (iii) Artificial limb.
Write the full form of AIDS and HIV.
AIDS: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus.
vsa: Explain any two major physical disabilities in children and one problem faced by each.
Blindness: the child cannot read or find the way, so needs Braille and a stick. Deafness: the child cannot hear his own voice so cannot learn language.

or: Explain how education helps a girl child in becoming a better mother in the future.
An educated girl can look after her children's studies and develop good habits and values. She understands their daily problems and gives meaningful solutions.

vsa: Imagine you are a teacher and notice a child labourer in your locality. What steps would you take to help the child return to school?
I would meet the parents and explain the harm of child labour and the value of education. I would arrange non-formal education and ask the employer to free the child for school.
Give three reasons why so much emphasis is being placed on educating girls.
It gives awareness and the ability to run the household efficiently. It gives financial independence and educated mothers raise better children.
Mention three ways in which poverty leads to juvenile delinquency.
Poor children lack facilities and find stealing easy. Parents may encourage them to steal or beg, and lack of play and education leads them into bad company.

or: Which three precautions should be adopted at the time of delivery?
A skilled person should be present at delivery and a hospital referral should be possible. The newborn must be kept clean, the cord tied and cut hygienically, and breast-feeding started early.

vsa: Define juvenile delinquency. Mention two delinquent behaviours.
It is violation of law by young people (a boy below 16 and a girl below 18). Examples are stealing and violence.
What is meant by child labour? State two causes.
It is work by children below 14 years to earn a living. Poverty and illiteracy of parents are causes.
sa: List various discriminations against the girl child.

(i) She is fed after the males and gets inadequate food, and is breast-fed for a shorter time. (ii) She is not taken to the doctor when sick, so many die in infancy. (iii) She is taken out of school early and made to do household chores.
Suggest preventive measures for juvenile delinquency (three points).

(i) Remove poverty through loans and vocational training. (ii) Parents should spend time with children and inculcate good habits and values. (iii) Provide recreational facilities and remand homes for reform and vocational training.
Explain the consequences of child labour (three points).
(i) Long hours in poor postures cause permanent disability. (ii) Unhygienic conditions cause infectious diseases. (iii) Missing school adds to illiteracy.
Explain how mentally retarded children can be helped (three points).
(i) Never call them stupid; let them do things themselves. (ii) Teach self-help skills and involve them in simple household tasks. (iii) Enrol them in special schools for vocational training.
List the modes of HIV transmission.

(i) Through infected blood and unsterilised needles, blades and instruments. (ii) From an infected mother to the child before or during birth and breast-feeding. (iii) Through unprotected sex with an infected partner.
la: Write a note on safe motherhood.

(i) Safe motherhood aims at reducing maternal mortality and morbidity. (ii) Avoid pregnancy before 18 and after 35–37 years. (iii) Plan the family with a gap of more than two years and two or three children. (iv) Use contraceptives: natural, mechanical (condom, Copper T), chemical or surgical. (v) Consult a qualified nurse or doctor in pregnancy and have a skilled person at delivery. (vi) Keep the newborn clean, tie the cord safely and start breast-feeding early.
